title: Former Pentagon spokesman on articles of impeachment filed against Hegseth
description: NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with former Pentagon spokesman John Ullyot about articles of impeachment brought against Secretary of Defense Pete H
body:
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with former Pentagon spokesman John Ullyot about articles of impeachment brought against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  John Ullyot has been listening to Tom with us and was also listening to Secretary Hegseth earlier. Ullyot is a longtime government spokesman in many roles, including in the White House during the first Trump administration. And he served briefly under Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon. He's since been a critic of the administration. Welcome back.JOHN ULLYOT: Thanks very much, Tom.INSKEEP: I just want to hear a little bit more of the defense secretary first.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PETE HEGSETH: For the first time in American history, a cabinet secretary overseeing America's military is being attacked not for losing conflicts with our enemies, but for winning them.INSKEEP: What do you make of that argument that Hegseth is under attack for winning?ULLYOT: Well, I think, first of all, this shows, if you take a step back about his bombastic approach that Tom Bowman was talking about, is that Secretary Hegseth always, when he's attacked, he hides behind the troops. And he says, well, this is an attack on the troops. This is an attack on the president. In that news conference, Tom - in that news conference, Steve, as Tom said, is that he's playing to an audience of one, and that's the president. He's looking into the camera, he's talking over the heads of reporters, and he is trying to impress the one person who controls his fate, which is the president.And as we've said before in our segment before the news conference, is that my view and the view of many others is that the president actually deserves better than this, especially going into the last two years of his presidency when, unlike the previous two years, there's actually going to be robust oversight of the secretary and of the Department of Defense. So the question is, in my view, the president deserves better than that because he is - because he can do better than having a bombastic secretary of defense for the next two years.INSKEEP: Let's talk that through. And, of course, you've just used the title of a book that's out today - happens to be authored by you - "The President Deserves Better." And you talk about this in a number of aspects. But it seems the president is very happy. We heard Leila quote him saying that Hegseth did an A-plus-plus-plus. I have to pause for a moment and note we're getting into the holiday season. People see the movie "Christmas Story," where the kid fantasizes about getting an A-plus-plus-plus-plus-plus. It's a fantasy. Pete Hegseth really got that grade from the president. You're saying the president is not being well served?ULLYOT: Well, the president is not well served because his aides need to tell him - and now it's probably up to Stephen Miller, who is his new chief of staff. And Stephen Miller has a reputation of also being a fire-breather, not quite as much as Pete Hegseth. But he's in a new role now, Stephen Miller. And he's got to tell the president, how can you advance your agenda? How can you get things done in the final two years? Is it with somebody who's going to be investigated top to bottom, if he's not impeached? And is it somebody who takes that bombastic approach?If you just - I mean, that was amazing, that news conference, because once again, he has this tone as if he's still on Fox News as a fire-breathing weekend cohost. And this is something that served him very well when he was at Fox News, in terms of becoming - moving up the ladder from just a correspondent to actually a cohost. And, look, he took that same attitude, even though Tom Bowman points out that he was confirmed by the slimmest of slim margins, 50-50, and then the vice president having to break the tie. And you'd think that somebody would come in there, after having that near-death experience for confirmation, and say, look, how can I pivot?What was it about my - I know he had a lot of personal baggage. But what can I do to just lower the temperature and have it not be about me? When he was at Fox News, it was good to have it about him and to be shouting into the microphone. And here, as we saw from this news conference today, that's a carbon copy from what he did whenever he gets out, because he only gets out - and he fenced off the press from the Pentagon.INSKEEP: Yeah.ULLYOT: First secretary who did that. And why doesn't he lower the temperature? That would be better. The president would be better served with that.INSKEEP: I think you're telling me, as someone who served in the Trump administration, who's conservative, who's Republican, you're saying that even if Hegseth believes he is innocent, that the wise, the practical thing to do would be to get out of the way?ULLYOT: Yes, absolutely. I think that if you're truly loyal to the president, as so many of us are - I was with him as a senior adviser on his 2016 campaign and all the way through his first term and a little bit of this term. You have to say, if you're truly loyal to the president and you become an issue, you become a target, then you should step out of the way because you're becoming baggage to the president. And he doesn't need that, especially going into the second term. I would argue that he didn't need that in most of the - sorry, last two years.I'd argue that he didn't need that in the last two years as well. I think he could've seen what was going on. He was very much - and I wrote about this in an op-ed, that the president was very much about accountability in the first term. He dismissed Tillerson. He dismissed...INSKEEP: Lots of firings. Sure.ULLYOT: Lots of firings after just one year. Whereas this is somebody who's been a real liability in terms of having a lot of baggage, being too bombastic, when the military is used to having very low-profile people, like Robert Gates, who's one of the most successful...INSKEEP: Oh, yeah. We talked about...ULLYOT: ...Secretaries. Exactly.INSKEEP: We talked about this earlier in the morning, that President George W. Bush, facing a controversial war, got rid of his defense secretary, who resigned, Rumsfeld, and was replaced by Gates, a more bipartisan figure. Now, I want to take seriously, though, this suggestion that you mentioned, Hegseth saying, if you come after me, you're coming after the troops; if I broke the law, the troops broke the law; if I committed war crimes, the troops committed war crimes. Let's just look at that for a moment. Do you believe that is accurate? If, as Thomas Massie says, this is an illegal war waged without proper authority from Congress, is everybody in the military guilty of a crime?ULLYOT: No. That's obviously a bogus accusation there because the troops are following lawful orders, or what they believe are lawful orders. And they're told by their commanders. And so nobody's going to be going after the troops or military. What the focus is here is on Secretary Hegseth, who's been, once again, a very divisive figure and has not, in my view, served the president well. But there are two particular actions that he took that possibly are criminal. One is sharing classified information with his wife over Signal. And she had no clearance whatsoever. By the way, that is exactly what John Bolton is being prosecuted by this Justice Department for doing.INSKEEP: Former national security adviser. Yeah.ULLYOT: Yeah, absolutely. And also, Petraeus did the same thing.INSKEEP: David Petraeus, yeah.ULLYOT: And he resigned. He was CIA director. And he resigned once it came to light that he shared classified information with somebody who wasn't authorized. So that's No. 1. No. 2 is this double-tap strike that he reportedly ordered personally, which is something where that's a violation of the laws of war. If you have somebody who surrenders and is essentially...INSKEEP: This is a second strike on a boat...ULLYOT: Second strike. And he apparently, reportedly, he ordered...INSKEEP: ...That had already been disabled or sunk...ULLYOT: He said, take them out, take them out right now. That is something that is absolutely a war crime and could be prosecuted. And then there are a bunch of other things. There's policy disagreements and everything else.INSKEEP: And the crime lies at his level...ULLYOT: Yeah. Nobody's going after...INSKEEP: ...Not at the level of some corporal somewhere?ULLYOT: Because he was the one who ordered that strike. Nobody's going after the people who pulled the trigger on that double strike because they were instructed, reportedly personally, by the secretary.INSKEEP: John Ullyot, senior Pentagon spokesman under Pete Hegseth and holder of other government positions, and author of "The President Deserves Better." Thanks for coming by.ULLYOT: Thank you, Steve.(SOUNDBITE OF ROY MARKSON'S "EVERYTHING IN IT'S RIGHT PLACE")

title: House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
description:
House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
    
            
                
                Transcript
body:
House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6036813/nx-s1-9999759" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10, 2026.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
    

   
   The House has voted 211 to 204 to refer the articles of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively killing the impeachment effort spearheaded by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.    Tuesday's vote short-circuits any potential floor vote on the articles of impeachment, and virtually guarantees the measure will not be taken up before the current session of Congress expires.    The vote provided a surprise reprieve for President Trump's embattled Defense Secretary, who was facing an impeachment vote by the full House as early as Wednesday.    Massie reintroduced the articles of impeachment on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors in connection to the war with Iran and U.S. strikes against Iran and on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean.    
   Massie's impeachment resolution sought to oust Hegseth over the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization, and the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for a video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders.    Hegseth defended himself against the impeachment effort during a rare press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday, criticizing Massie as a "disgruntled and defeated congressman."    "I stand behind every one of these operations," Hegseth said. "I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow."   On Monday, Trump expressed support for Hegseth during a wide-ranging, impromptu press briefing at the White House.    "I'll stand by him," Trump said. "He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won."   The impeachment measure was Massie's second attempt against Hegseth. He first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections, prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution again this week.    While the impeachment push may be quelled for now, Hegseth's troubles on Capitol Hill are not over. Democrats have promised vigorous investigations into Hegseth's Pentagon once they assume the majority in January.    
   Whether they will mount another impeachment effort remains unclear, but in an interview with NPR last week, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next Speaker of the House, said simply of Hegseth, "He's got to go."

title: The Democratic Party gained power across the country in the midterms. Now what?
description: Newly elected Democratic U.S. senators h
body:
Newly elected Democratic U.S. senators head toward an orientation meeting inside the U.S. Capitol on Monday. From left to right are Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, James Talarico of Texas, Josh Turek of Iowa and Troy Jackson of Maine.
                
                    Win McNamee/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Win McNamee/Getty Images
    

   
   Two years ago, voters sent Democrats a message when they ousted them from power in Washington. At first glance, last week's midterm results sent a new one.   Democrats will enter the next Congress with one of the largest majorities in a generation, flipping dozens of House districts and at least seven Senate seats in mainly Trump-won communities. The party now controls a majority of governorships, and gained control of several additional state legislative chambers.   "I think one of the big surprises for me on Tuesday night was just how deep and wide our election results were," Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin said in an interview with NPR. "This was the biggest election cycle for Democrats in the history of our party."   
   Martin, who has faced criticism from some inside the party throughout his term as chairman, said that the stunning Democratic victories across the country were the result of his party's focus on issues like affordability and ending the war in Iran.   He said the midterms were bigger than politics and bigger than party, and acknowledged the results were just as much about serving as a "massive repudiation of Donald Trump and the MAGA Trumpers and the Republican Party." "I think it's an admonition for Democrats, for sure: Now that we're in power, we have to deliver," he said. "But it was a complete message to Republicans. You had the ability to help us and you did nothing."   Blue tsunami in the South   With an expanded congressional majority and a lame duck president, one of the frontlines for figuring out if the Democratic Party's power will hold will be in the South, Martin said.   "Six of the 10 fastest-growing parts of the country right now are below the Mason-Dixon line, and 40% of the U.S. population is going to live in the South after the next census," he said. "As we go into 2032 and there's a realignment with the reapportionment, states like Minnesota, Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, New York, Rhode Island, Illinois and California are all going to lose electoral votes and congressional votes to the South."   
   Last week's midterms brought the region's power — especially with Black voters — more squarely into focus. Turbocharged Black voter turnout helped elect the country's first Black female governor in Georgia and may elect the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction.   A slew of Republican-led states seeking to redraw House maps for partisan advantage backfired, as Democrats gained several seats across the region.   Georgia Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock said in an interview with NPR that Democratic victories in 2026 were a "proof of concept" that the South is central to the future of American politics.   "You saw a multiracial coalition of voters stand up on Tuesday night beyond anything I had even hoped for, and they offered a silent rebuke of where we are now," he told NPR. "It's now up to us to provide the leadership, even as we listen to people, and point the way forward into how we build an economy that works for everyday working families."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference on Nov. 4 in Washington, D.C. Jeffries is expected to be the next speaker of the House, the first Black speaker in history.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
    

   
   Warnock said Democrats' direction in the next two years should aim to serve as a cure for the last decade of Trump-dominated politics that has been defined more as top versus bottom rather than left versus right.   "Ordinary people have had their hopes dashed time and time again, cycle after cycle, across Republican and Democratic administrations," he said. "They've seen the widening chasm between the haves and the have nots."   He called the midterms a "moral moment" that will help determine what kind of nation America wants to be.   Looking ahead to 2028   In the early days after the 2026 elections, a look ahead to the 2028 presidential race finds both parties with the potential to see crowded fields of candidates in several new lanes reacting to signals sent by the electorate.   That includes Warnock, who will be up for reelection in 2028 and is among names floated as a presidential contender, along with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Rep. Ro Khanna, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, former Vice President Kamala Harris and others who have spent significant time in the South campaigning for other Democrats.   
   As new members of Congress descend on Washington for their orientations, competing visions for Democratic governance are on display with postmortem event panels called "What Worked" and "What Just Happened?" and event names like "What's Next" as party strategists argue online about which wing of the party was the most successful.   2026 victories also scramble the traditional map of swing states, Martin said, suggesting that Democrats would start off competitive in places like Florida and Texas and as favorites to win the White House.   "Texas is no longer a red state. It is a blue state. They didn't even go from red to purple to blue, which is a normal sort of progression," he said. "If Texas is now a blue state, and you look at Georgia and you look at other parts of the South, how do the Republicans get to 270 votes?"

title: Hegseth has remained defiant as Congress members deliberate articles of impeachment
description: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is fighting back. As members of Congress begin deliberating on the articles of impeachment against him, Hegseth
body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is fighting back. As members of Congress begin deliberating on the articles of impeachment against him, Hegseth gave his first press conference in months.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:  Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is fighting back. On the same day members of Congress began voting on the articles of impeachment against him, he gave his first press conference in six months. Hegseth argues that the impeachment effort is a political stunt.(SOUNDBITE OF PRESS CONFERENCE)PETE HEGSETH: Let's be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies - Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching - that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.PFEIFFER: With us now to talk about the latest on this is NPR's Pentagon correspondent Tom Bowman, sitting across from me in the studio. Hi, Tom.TOM BOWMAN, BYLINE: Hey there.PFEIFFER: And NPR's media correspondent David Folkenflik on the line. Hi, David.DAVID FOLKENFLIK, BYLINE: Hey, Sacha.PFEIFFER: Tom, tell us more about how Hegseth is trying to hold on to his position, the case he's making to the media and to the public.BOWMAN: Well, first of all, he was his usual combative self. And again, he said all these missions were - military missions were lawful. And he noted that past presidents were never called to task for their own operations that some question whether they violated the War Powers Act. Most of these impeachment articles had to do with the wars in Iran and Yemen. By the way, he called Congressman Thomas Massie a disgruntled, defeated congressman, and talk of impeachment is a farce, a show trial.PFEIFFER: And Tom, the specific impeachment articles, how is he defending himself against them? For example, that he killed civilians, that he acted outside the authority of position when the U.S. arrested Venezuela's president, when it's been striking, bombing the suspected drug boats.BOWMAN: Well, again, he says, again, all these were legal missions. And on the alleged drug boats, he said the U.S. has sunk more than 70 of what he called narcoterrorist boats and killed 218 narcoterrorists. So he's saying not civilians. But it's important, Sacha, to note the Coast Guard has estimated that in about one-quarter of the boats in the area they interdict, no drugs were found. So one of the articles of impeachment refers to what it calls, you know, these illegal killings. And in one case, two survivors on a boat were also killed by U.S. service members. Some legal analysts are saying this article may have some political weight, more heft on Capitol Hill because it concerns specific charges.Another one, Sacha, with the weight - legal weight - concerns Hegseth's effort to investigate Senator Mark Kelly for appearing on a video reminding service members they don't have to obey illegal orders. A federal judge said that violated Kelly's First Amendment rights.PFEIFFER: David, one of the things you do as our media correspondent is not just study the content of what people say, but let's call it the stagecraft of it, their speech. How did Hegseth's demeanor strike you?FOLKENFLIK: Well, I'd say he was tense and intense. And what was clear is throughout his remarks he wrapped himself in President Trump and in the troops as though he was their shield and their protector. Here's a soundbite of what I mean.(SOUNDBITE OF PRESS CONFERENCE)HEGSETH: Put the secretary on trial today and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow. If they want to come for the warriors, they're going to have to come through me.FOLKENFLIK: But if you really listen to what he had to say, Sacha, that seemed like an inversion of what was happening. He wanted to use them to shield him. And Secretary Hegseth really seemed only to get his full footing as he was asked questions by these completely onside pro-Trump media figures in the room.PFEIFFER: David, as you know, this is the secretary's first briefing in a long time. What other types of questions was he asked?FOLKENFLIK: Well, to be fair, look, I thought Lucas Tomlinson of Fox News asked about Vice President Vance's remarks in which he blamed the war against Iran for the midterm results for Republicans. And that, you know, was a question I think a lot of people wanted to hear how the defense secretary would answer. But a lot of the other questions, you've seen tougher pitches in T-ball leagues. You know, how does it make you feel when your own party's politicians aren't supporting you? Boy, it sounds like you're comfortable in the president's support. What do you think about the appointment of Steve Miller as the new chief of staff? Have you rallied allies on Capitol Hill?He called on either conservative news outlets, including The Washington Times, or outright MAGA press figures. And let's remember, the secretary had essentially insisted that reporters had to formally pledge not to report anything unauthorized in order to continue covering the military from the Pentagon itself. And dozens of news outlets, including those across the political spectrum, walked away.PFEIFFER: And Tom, that pledge that David just mentioned, NPR was among the media outlets that refused to sign it. What have the effects of that been?BOWMAN: Well, it's much harder to cover the Pentagon. There are no real briefings, almost no background briefings. We're all still have to contact - well, you still have contacts in the Pentagon, but they're shut out of detailed information as well. And, you know, this lack of transparency really is helping no one. Not the American public, not the military out in the field. I remember Hal Moore, a retired general who served in Vietnam, once saying to me, I always took reporters with me on combat missions because the American people have a right to know what's being done in their name. I think that's lost.FOLKENFLIK: You know, let's acknowledge at a time when impeachment articles are being filed, at a time of war, you know, at times of crisis, those are moments at which public officials seek to need to face the music, face the questions. And, you know, essentially, you've seen this administration, the defense secretary, the president seek to avoid those questions and seek to prevent and pressure news outlets from asking ones they don't want to face.PFEIFFER: That's NPR media correspondent David Folkenflik and Pentagon correspondent Tom Bowman. Thanks to both of you.BOWMAN: You're welcome.FOLKENFLIK: You bet.

title: House Republicans elect Jim Jordan as their next leader
description: House GOP lawmakers have chosen Ohio's Jim Jordan to serve as minority leader, elevating a co-founder of the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus
body:
House GOP lawmakers have chosen Ohio's Jim Jordan to serve as minority leader, elevating a co-founder of the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus to succeed Mike Johnson as the chamber's top Republican.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:  Republicans in Congress are working to put the pieces back together again after last week's losses in the midterm elections. Today, they took an important first step by electing new leaders in the House and Senate ahead of Democrats assuming the majority. Here is Ohio's Jim Jordan, who was elected to serve as a minority leader in the House.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JIM JORDAN: Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump, every single day.PFEIFFER: NPR congressional correspondent Claudia Grisales is on Capitol Hill covering this and joins me now. Hi, Claudia.CLAUDIA GRISALES, BYLINE: Hey, Sacha.PFEIFFER: Let's start with the House with Jim Jordan as minority leader. Tell us a little miniature biography of him.GRISALES: Yes, he's a former college wrestling coach, and he's brought kind of a hard-charging style to these fights with Democrats that he's had. And that's what a lot of Republicans said they were looking for in the fallout after the midterm election losses. He also cofounded the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus and served as the top Republican on the House Oversight Committee when they were in the minority.Jordan was most recently chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. That's where he helped lead a two-year impeachment probe into former President Biden. Ultimately, Republicans did not pursue impeachment, but he also investigated former Special Counsel Jack Smith and Democratic officials who had challenged President Trump. And these committees he served on - House oversight and judiciary - they're poised to play a central role in the new Congress as Democrats plan for a long list of investigations into President Trump and his administration.PFEIFFER: Who did Jordan beat out for the job?GRISALES: Well, he defeated Louisiana's Steve Scalise. He currently serves as the No. 2 House Republican behind Johnson. He did this in a vote of 106 to 73.PFEIFFER: And, Claudia, a bigger picture question - what do you think Jordan's win signals about the direction House Republicans will go in the minority?GRISALES: Well, they wanted a fresh face at the top. And Jordan in his pitch to his colleagues said that for too long, the conferences operated without a, quote, "clear plan to survive the next hour or day in front of us" - so clearly, a hit on the current leadership team that included Scalise. And he said that kind of approach won't work with emboldened Democrats. And they're coming in with a significant margin in the House, and that's going to leave Republicans with little leverage to shift the floor agenda.PFEIFFER: That's the House. If we move to the Senate, what did Republicans decide there?GRISALES: Well, that was a less of a surprise. Senate Majority Leader John Thune will become minority leader, as (ph) he's held the top job since last year after succeeding his predecessor, Mitch McConnell. He has sometimes had a tense relationship with President Trump, who was frustrated with Thune for failing to push through his long-sought voting restriction bill and ending the filibuster. But Thune has a lot of support inside the conference, and he did not even have a challenger.PFEIFFER: Claudia, what about the Democrats? What are some of the key things you think we should know about their leadership races?GRISALES: Well, they have more time to reflect on their decision. House Democrats will vote next week. In that case, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker in history.PFEIFFER: And could things play out as easily for Senate Democrats?GRISALES: Well, maybe not. Today, Vermont Independent Senator Bernie Sanders - he caucuses with Democrats. He became one of the more high-profile senators to call for new leadership at the top, but it's unclear who could challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who seemed to be on an easy track to become majority leader, especially as Senate Democrats blew past expectations with their wins, and they're on track to have a comfortable majority.PFEIFFER: That is NPR congressional correspondent Claudia Grisales. Thank you.GRISALES: Thank you.

title: House GOP faults the federal government for failing to hold Epstein accountable
description: The House Oversight Committee has released a report into its investigation into sex-offender, Jeffrey Epstein. They faulted the federal governm
body:
The House Oversight Committee has released a report into its investigation into sex-offender, Jeffrey Epstein. They faulted the federal government for not holding the financier accountable.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:  It's been more than a year since the House Oversight Committee launched its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Today, the Republican-led committee published its report on that investigation, and the report puts a lot of blame on the federal government for a decades-long failure to hold Epstein accountable for his crimes. NPR's Ava Berger has been reading that report, and she's with me now in the studio. Hi, Ava.AVA BERGER, BYLINE: Hi, Sacha.PFEIFFER: I assume this is not a short report, but could you recap it for us?BERGER: I can. It is not short. It's 136 pages. It's a hard read, Sacha. It's based on 19 interviews and depositions with some big names that we've heard before - the Clintons, Bill Gates, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. There's two big takeaways. First, the report blames the federal government for mishandling the investigations into Epstein, like you said. And second, it says the Department of Justice needs to interview or reinterview key witnesses. I mean, basically, start this investigation again. Here's the chair of the committee, James Comer, in a social media video posted today. He's a Republican from Kentucky.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JAMES COMER: The Department of Justice must interview key witnesses, investigate everyone who participated in or facilitated these crimes and provide survivors access to their records. Congress could investigate, but it cannot deliver justice alone.BERGER: This is notable, Sacha, because right now the oversight committee is led by Republicans. And this is them taking a strong stance on the investigation into the convicted sex offender, even to go as far as to say that Trump's DOJ failed to protect survivors when they released the Epstein files. In many cases, their personal information was made public.PFEIFFER: Any response from the DOJ on these charges levied against it?BERGER: Yes, the DOJ told NPR in a statement today that they have already addressed these recommendations put forward by the report and that the Epstein case is not closed.PFEIFFER: As we have talked about repeatedly before on our air, President Trump's name has come up repeatedly in the Epstein files. Did the report today say anything about him?BERGER: Yes. It said that from everything they found, these interviews in this investigation, Trump was not implicated in any of Epstein's crimes. This lines up with what the president has said many times before. The report also said that Democrats have made this process political by insinuating Trump's connection with Epstein and his crimes. You can see there where the Republicans and Democrats on the committee differ. Robert Garcia, he's the lead Democrat on the committee, he said in a statement that today's report was partisan and incomplete.PFEIFFER: Ava, if you've been able to reach any survivors of Epstein's abuse, how are they reacting to the report?BERGER: Yeah, I talked with Dani Bensky today. She says that when she was 17, Epstein abused her as a young dancer. She's been speaking out with other survivors. She wants the DOJ to keep investigating and look into some of the people named in the report. But she also said the report gives her hope.DANI BENSKY: I do feel hopeful. I mean, to us, it's never been partisan, and it's never been a Democrat versus Republican thing. It's always been whoever will follow the evidence wherever it goes is who we will support and where we'll land.BERGER: Bensky and other survivors will actually be on the Hill next week to mark one year since the Epstein Transparency Act was signed. That was that unanimous Senate vote that ordered the DOJ to release the millions of Epstein files to the public.PFEIFFER: The midterms, as we know, have changed control of the House, and as a result, in January, the Democrats will lead the oversight committee. What will they do differently, if anything?BERGER: Robert Garcia, who I mentioned before, he will likely be the leader of the committee. He says that under the Democrats' leadership, the committee will hold hearings in public, which they have not done before, and they say they will continue to question powerful men associated with Epstein, including Trump. He, Garcia, has also emphasized that he wants the survivors of Epstein's abuse, like Bensky, to be at the center of this work.PFEIFFER: That's NPR's Ava Berger. Thank you.BERGER: Thanks, Sacha.(SOUNDBITE OF POST MALONE SONG, "CHEMICAL")

title: Why did California's billionaire tax fail to surf the blue wave?
body:
Ultrasound Technologist Mayra Castaneda speaks in front of healthcare workers holding placards in support of the Billionaire Tax during a media briefing in Los Angeles on April 27, 2026. Healthcare workers and allies outlined the next steps in their effort to get California's Billionaire Tax on the ballot for the November election, with their efforts already exceeding 1,500,000 signatures collected from across the state. The initiative would levy a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires. (Photo by Frederic J. BROWN / AFP via Getty Images)
                
                    FREDERIC J. BROWN/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        FREDERIC J. BROWN/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
    

   
   Late Monday, The Associated Press determined that California voters had rejected Prop 40, the proposed billionaire wealth tax I wrote about last week. Given the big blue wave we saw during the midterms, why did this tax on billionaires fail to surf to victory?   To make sense of the results, I went back to the two economists I spoke with last week: UC Berkeley's Gabriel Zucman, a leading champion of wealth taxes, and Stanford's Joshua Rauh, a prominent critic of Prop 40.   Last week, they disagreed on what this wealth tax on billionaires would do to California's economy and tax revenue. Now comes the sequel, in which they disagree on what the results say about the politics of wealth taxes.   
   Their debate could foreshadow a bigger one in the next Democratic presidential primary: should the party embrace a wealth tax?   Did billionaire money tip the scales?   Zucman blames the corrosive influence of money for Prop 40's failure.   "I am not surprised," Zucman says. Opponents of Prop 40 spent almost $400 million fighting it, including spending on competing ballot measures, making it one of the most expensive ballot initiative fights in history.   "The money spent by the billionaires was critical," Zucman says. "Anyone who lives in California has been carpet-bombed by a deluge of ads. One can easily see how this could be pivotal in such a closely contested ballot."   But didn't Democrats win plenty of races this cycle despite huge sums spent against them? In Texas, for example, Elon Musk alone poured more than $150 million into defeating Democrat James Talarico. And Talarico ended up winning his Senate race by a comfortable margin. Why would money have been so decisive with Prop 40 and not in other races around the nation?   For one, Zucman says, the spending gap was much bigger in the fight over Prop 40. "The billionaires spent more than $300 million on ads versus negligible sums on the other side," Zucman says. "On TV and in their mailboxes, voters were exposed only to the anti-tax arguments. This was very different from the other midterm races: in those races, when spending was high (e.g., Talarico vs. Paxton in Texas) it was high on both sides, even if unevenly. The net difference in spending was considerably larger for Prop 40."   
   It's also possible that money can matter more in ballot initiatives than in races between candidates. Analysts have complained for decades that California's ballot initiative system is too easily manipulated by special interest groups. The nitty-gritty details of specific policies can get complicated, and many voters don't take the time to get educated on them. That can give well-funded advertising campaigns more power to shape their views.   In candidate races, meanwhile, voters can at least fall back on name recognition or party labels, which give them an easy mental shortcut — what social scientists call a "heuristic" — when making decisions at the ballot box. Even when they know little about the candidates, they usually know which party they prefer.   But Prop 40 didn't come with the same clear partisan signal. In fact, prominent Democrats, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, came out against it. Newsom said he favored a national minimum tax on billionaires instead.   Or was this tax policy itself the problem?   "Popular opinion on wealth taxes is clearly not as strong as proponents thought," Rauh says.   Rauh questions whether money and advertising can really explain Prop 40's poor showing. He compared support for the tax with support for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. In some of "the most progressive Bay Area counties," he says, Harris won overwhelming support while Prop 40 won much less. This gap between support for Harris and support for Prop 40 was bigger there than it was in other Democratic-leaning counties across the state.   If advertising was the main explanation for this tax's poor showing, he argues, why was the gap so much bigger in the Bay Area? Sure, he says, advertisers may have done more targeting there, but he thinks the uneven pattern across the state casts doubt on the idea that advertising was the decisive factor.   
   "[T]he counties with the largest defections are actually the ones whose residents are most likely to know a billionaire, to work for one, or to have watched one move to Texas or Florida," Rauh writes in a recent post. "The simple reading is that proximity to the people being taxed, and to the businesses they fund, made voters more skeptical of the tax relative to their baseline politics."   For Rauh, that skepticism points to a broader conclusion: "The electorate even in progressive California has shown that it isn't ready for a wealth tax," he says.   More moderate Democratic voters, especially in affluent areas like the Bay Area, may simply dislike this novel way of taxing rich people in America and the consequences it could have. After all, this policy idea has divided Democrats before. During the 2020 presidential primary, Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders both championed wealth taxes, but rivals like Sen. Cory Booker and Michael Bloomberg opposed them. Joe Biden said he didn't oppose a wealth tax on the campaign trail, but early in his presidency, he declined to pursue Sen. Warren's wealth tax proposal.   Or maybe voters weren't rejecting the idea of a wealth tax per se. Maybe they were rejecting the particulars of this wealth tax.   For one thing, Prop 40 was a one-time tax, and it earmarked its projected revenue in ways that drew opposition from traditional Democratic allies. It allocated 90% of the revenue to health care, leaving only 10% for food assistance and education-related programs.   That helped put some typically left-leaning organizations in the opposition camp. For example, the California Teachers Association, a powerful teachers union. It argued that Prop 40 shortchanged public schools and did "not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve."   Meanwhile, Prop 40 would have taxed billionaires at the state level. Supporters of a national approach argue that a wealth tax would be more effective at the national level because it's harder to leave America than it is to move to another state.   
   When Newsom came out against Prop 40 back in June, he wrote, "Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level, where this broken system was created in the first place."   Where does the wealth tax movement go from here?   Despite Prop 40's defeat, Zucman believes the wealth tax movement is far from over.   "With the blue wave nationally, the billionaire tax is going to be front and center in the new Congress," Zucman says. "Many of the newly elected Democratic senators have been campaigning on curbing the power and influence of billionaires. One can reasonably expect to see significant progress in the next two years."   Rauh also expects to see more wealth tax proposals in the coming Congress. But with President Trump in the White House, he sees little chance of one becoming law anytime soon.   "It will be the 2028 election that will really demonstrate the extent to which the public wants wealth taxation, as those proposals will likely feature prominently in political debate," Rauh says.   But even if wealth tax supporters win over voters, Rauh stresses they would encounter another big hurdle: the courts. He argues a federal wealth tax would constitute "a direct tax," a kind of tax that is subject to crippling constitutional restrictions.   As I explained in this 2019 Planet Money newsletter, the U.S. Constitution requires that "direct taxes" go through a complicated rigamarole in order to be constitutional. Specifically, the share of a direct tax's total revenue collected from each state has to match its share of the national population. That could mean wildly different tax rates depending on where people live.   This weird rule's history is tangled up with slavery. In one early Supreme Court case, one justice described it as basically a concession to Southern states seeking to limit federal taxation of their land and enslaved people.   
   The 16th Amendment exempted income taxes from this requirement. But that amendment doesn't mention wealth taxes.   Legal scholars disagree over whether this rule would doom a federal wealth tax. Is a wealth tax even a "direct tax"? That early Supreme Court case involved a tax on horse-drawn carriages that George Washington signed into law in 1794. The Court upheld it, a precedent wealth tax supporters point to today. For more on that story, listen to the Planet Money episode I did, "The Carriage Tax."   Stay tuned for more wealth tax coverage in the Planet Money newsletter in the future. We guess this movement isn't going away.

schema.headline: Why did California's billionaire tax fail to surf the blue wave?

title: Supreme Court seems split over federal agencies' ability to fine for law violations
description: The U.S. Capitol is seen behind signage
body:
The U.S. Capitol is seen behind signage for U.S. Department of Labor in Washington, D.C., in August 2025.
                
                    Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   At the Supreme Court, the justices seemed divided on Tuesday in a case that could undermine the ability of many federal regulatory agencies to fine businesses that violate federal laws.   For decades, farmers have relied on a federal immigration program that allows them to temporarily employ migrant workers to pick crops.   In addition to wages, farm owners must provide basic necessities, such as housing, access to meals and water. The whole system is essentially policed by the Department of Labor to ensure that foreign workers don't undercut domestic laborers.   
   In that role, the department fined Sun Valley Orchards, based in New Jersey, a half-million dollars for unsanitary conditions, including providing unsafe drinking water, housing people in 20-bunk rooms, broken sinks and other violations, including failure to pay promised wages.   Sun Valley is disputing the charges and contends that the Department of Labor imposing monetary fines based on its administrative proceedings is unconstitutional. Sun Valley also says the process denies them the right to a jury trial when and if they appeal to a federal court.   At the high court Tuesday, Chief Justice John Roberts strongly suggested that the Trump administration, and many administrations before it, have exceeded the power of the executive branch. In this case, potentially wading into the judicial branch's territory.   Addressing Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who represented the Labor Department, Roberts said, "It seems to me you're just trying to leverage … the broad authority [of the executive branch] beyond the justification for its application."   
   Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked how disruptive it would be for the federal courts to enforce the law instead of the designated agency (in this case the Department of Labor).   Harris responded succinctly, "If the court were to say civil penalties always have to be in Article III courts, that's kind of the nuclear option."   Harris added that such a ruling would disrupt programs as diverse as Medicare, Medicaid, the federal student loan program and more.   That prompted this question from Justice Elena Kagan: "Why not just go to court always?" Harris quickly responded, "I think it would be catastrophic." She went on to explain that a system like that would inevitably result in massive under-enforcement of the law, given limited resources.   
   Lawyer Robert Johnson represented Sun Valley Orchards. "To be sure," he said, "the statute contemplates penalties, but it says nothing about where those penalties should be adjudicated."   
   Johnson further contended that penalties should be imposed by the federal courts, not the administrative agencies that do most of that work under current law.   To that Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson replied, "It seems like you're just sort of fighting the reality of … what Congress was trying to do … in ensuring that we don't have farm workers coming in and undercutting domestic workers."   A more skeptical observation came from Justice Brett Kavanaugh: "What you're proposing is really at war with clarity," he said, adding, "I think that's not great systematically going forward."   Justice Samuel Alito pointedly added, "What you're outlining is sort of a hodge-podge opinion, and maybe sometimes courts write that sort of thing," to which Justice Kagan quickly chimed in with a chuckling crowd in the court, "Not ever us!"   
   In rebuttal, Deputy Solicitor General Harris was unusually candid. "It would be a big deal for the government to lose, but an even bigger deal would be to have a mess," she said. She later added, "A lot of other statutory regimes also would be on the cutting-room floor."   And if that's the case, she said, the administration will have to go to Congress. Her voice rising, she added, "Please tell us now ... if we need to get Legislative Affairs on it right now, because this will snowball."

title: House set to vote to impeach Hegseth. And, SCOTUS allows border wall work to proceed
description: Hegseth Impeachment Push, Trump Holds Off Iran Strikes, Congress Summons Nvidia's CEO
body:
Hegseth Impeachment Push, Trump Holds Off Iran Strikes, Congress Summons Nvidia's CEO
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-152777/nx-s1-mx-6035504-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   The House may vote this week on a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-KY, reintroduced articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors. The eight specific charges include three charges for illegally waging war against Iran, one for ignoring laws to minimize civilian casualties, one for overseeing extrajudicial killings of alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, and one for capturing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization. Hegseth has called the articles a sham.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY), seen here on September 16, 2026 at the U.S. Capitol, filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday.
                
                    Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
    

   
   🎧 Only a few Republicans need to support impeachment in the House for it to be possible, NPR's Sam Gringlas tells Up First. This would lead to a Senate trial. Removing Hegseth from the Pentagon requires 67 senators, which will be challenging even once Democrats take control. But Massie told reporters he believes it will be possible, and opposition to the war in his fellow Republicans' home states could convince them to get on board. Massie says some members of Congress have come around to the idea that the administration must be held accountable for violating congressional war powers➡️ Also on House Republicans' agenda: a closed-door meeting today to pick a minority leader for the next Congress. The decision is down to current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., and Ohio's Jim Jordan, a co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus.   
   President Trump has acknowledged that the war he initiated with Iran harmed his party in the midterms. Weeks before the election, the president said he was going to hold off on any strikes in Iran. While campaigning, he hinted at potential actions to proceed with the war and teased a significant move to end it. Now, Trump says there's no need for further strikes if talks are ongoing.   🎧 NPR's Deepa Shivaram says it's possible that Trump might resume military action if he doesn't get the deal he wants, because he has shown a pattern of shifting on his rhetoric since the war began. The president has also insisted that the war was necessary and he would do it again. Shivaram says Trump is starting to shift focus to shape his legacy in these last two years of his presidency. He is trying to frame the unpopular war as a success by saying Iran's nuclear stock is eliminated and that was his goal. In the remainder of his time in office, he wants to establish himself as a dealmaker and peacemaker.   Nvidia's stock slipped around 4.25% after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. This news sent shockwaves from Wall Street to Capitol Hill. AMD, Nvidia's main AI chip competitor, saw its shares jump more than 13%.   
   🎧 Nvidia is central to the U.S.-China competition over AI, which could make Huang's statements and actions of high interest to Beijing, NPR's John Ruwitch says. The woman Huang admitted to having an affair with is an executive at MegaSpeed, a Singapore-based company that Nvidia has collaborated with. The controversy centers around whether MegaSpeed was helping Chinese firms bypass chip export controls. The New York Times reports that the U.S. Commerce Department is investigating MegaSpeed and that the woman was giving information to Beijing. NPR has not independently verified these claims.   The U.S. Supreme Court yesterday gave the Trump administration the green light to proceed with plans to build hundreds of miles of border barriers and security infrastructure in west Texas. The decision was made despite ongoing court hearings. This plan has faced bipartisan backlash for its involvement of Big Bend National Park, a cherished area known for its stunning canyons and pristine desert landscape. In a five-page decision, the Court asserted that the federal judge who issued an injunction against the construction lacked the authority to intervene.   Deep dive   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                James Talarico speaks on election night in Austin, Texas. Talarico won his race for U.S. Senate by 12 percentage points overall, but when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
    

   
   Democrats did really well with Gen Z voters in last week's midterm election, snagging nearly a 50-point lead among voters under 30. This is a major comeback from 2024, when young voters leaned toward Trump. This year's results signal that the youngest generation of voters are issuing a strong rebuke of Republicans, and they're ready to fight for an American dream that feels just out of reach. Here's how Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave:   🌊 Americans ages 18-29 have historically voted at lower rates than older voters. But this year, Gen Z accounted for 11% of the total vote. In the Texas Senate race, Democrat James Talarico won by 12 percentage points. Among Gen Z voters, he won by 60 points.🌊 Democrats credit their strong slate of candidates for boosting enthusiasm, but strong opposition to Trump also played a key role.🌊 Democrats gained support from some young voters who backed Trump two years ago, including white and Latino men. Both blocs voted blue by double digits this year. The party also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and those without college degrees.🌊 Some gains may have been influenced by young Trump voters who chose not to participate in this election, but it's unclear how many of them there were.   
   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A wild horse grazes on whatever food it can find on Cumberland Island, Ga on Oct 8, 2026. The National Park Service, which has managed the island since 1972, recently proposed a land-swap with the descendants of Thomas Carnegie,  the wealthy Gilded Age industrialist who built homes on the island.
                
                    Malcolm Jackson for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Malcolm Jackson for NPR
    

   
   Visitors, ecologists, park rangers and residents all cherish Cumberland Island, Ga., but they often disagree on the best ways to protect it. Feral horses, hogs and deer roam freely across the 18-mile island. Since 1972, Congress has mandated the preservation of thousands of wilderness acres under National Park Service protection. The island showcases a rich human history, including Native American artifacts, Spanish missions and grand Gilded Age mansions from the Carnegie era. Today, descendants of industrialist Thomas Carnegie still reside on private property. Now, a park service land-swap proposal with the family could greenlight new construction. The new development could ignite a clash among stakeholders over what true island preservation actually looks like.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, called Harrison a "a genuinely original thinker, a genre-defying writer who takes ideas seriously."
                
                    Yuki Sugiura/The Booker Prize Foundation
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Yuki Sugiura/The Booker Prize Foundation
    

   
   M. John Harrison's The End of Everything has won the 2026 Booker Prize. It follows Philip, who searches for "artifacts" along the coast of Kent, England, in a post-apocalyptic future.British comedian Russell Brand has been sentenced to more than 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.For his efforts to challenge menstrual stigma, 18-year-old Aadvik Jain is one of this year's recipients of the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities.   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: House GOP elects Jim Jordan as new leader as the party looks to rebuild from midterms
description: Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, is seen ahead of a m
body:
Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, is seen ahead of a meeting Tuesday with House Republicans, where they elected their party's leadership for the 120th Congress. Jordan emerged from a two-man contest victorious, and will lead Republicans as they navigate life in the minority.
                
                    Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   House Republicans on Tuesday selected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to serve as the party's next minority leader.    In Jordan, 62, Republicans have chosen a veteran of both the House Oversight and House Judiciary committees — two panels poised to play a central role in the new Congress as Democrats plan for a long list of investigations into President Trump and his administration.   
   Jordan, a co-founder of the ultra-conservative House Freedom Caucus, won the vote over current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La. He will succeed Mike Johnson, R-La., as the top House Republican when the new Congress begins in January.    The election, conducted via secret ballot, offered rank-and-file Republicans a choice as to how they want to navigate life in the minority, as they look to regroup from a staggering defeat that saw Democrats flip more than 40 GOP seats.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, left, and Rep. Steve Scalise, R-La., confer during a news conference at the Capitol in Washington, Wednesday, June 8, 2022. The two GOP leaders have emerged as contenders for the top Republican post in the House after losing the majority to Democrats in the midterm elections.
                
                    J. Scott Applewhite/AP/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        J. Scott Applewhite/AP/AP
    

   
   A former college wrestling coach known for his pugilistic style, Jordan pitched an aggressive posture to his colleagues, writing that "offense, not defense, wins elections."   
   "For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democratic party," Jordan said in a letter to colleagues last week, taking a swipe at the House leadership team led by Johnson and Scalise.   "I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats' playbook," he added.   
   The House Freedom Caucus celebrated Jordan's win, calling him a "fierce fighter."   "Jim is exactly the right man for the job to fight back against the radical, crazy agenda of Democrats," Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., said in a statement.    Jordan's pitch stood in contrast to what Scalise, 61, offered. Scalise has been the No. 2 House Republican since 2023, and has served in broader GOP leadership roles for more than 10 years. He's seen as more moderate than Jordan, and in a letter to colleagues announcing his candidacy, the close Trump ally said his approach to the job would be "conservative and consensus-driven."   "My number one goal as Republican Leader will be to win back the majority and I expect you to hold me accountable to that mission," Scalise wrote. "To succeed, we will need to be effective in both the oversight and legislative fights ahead, but we will also need to lay out a clear and optimistic vision for America."   
   The contest between Jordan and Scalise was a rematch from 2023. Back then, Jordan and Scalise were vying to succeed Kevin McCarthy. After multiple candidates failed to secure enough votes, Republicans ultimately voted for Johnson.   
   Speaking ahead of the vote, John Leganski, who was an aide to McCarthy, said the size of Democrats' victory last week will limit the next minority leader's leverage in the new Congress.    "I think whoever wins your job is to … number one, try to win back to the House," he said. "And number two, make life as difficult for the Democrats as possible, largely by voting no."   Continuity in the Senate   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Sen. John Thune, R-S.D., speaks to reporters at the Capitol on Sept. 29, 2026.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
    

   
   In the Senate, Republicans opted for continuity over change, electing Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to a second term as party leader.    Thune has faced criticism from Trump over the last two years for refusing to eliminate the Senate filibuster and failing to pass his long-sought election overhaul bill, the SAVE America Act.    Despite that, Thune enjoyed broad support inside the GOP caucus, and ran unopposed in Tuesday's election.    "I'm proud of what this Republican team has accomplished together, and we remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats' efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda," Thune said in a statement after the vote.
